Photograph: Andrew Aitchison/The Guardian Immigration and asylum On the ground in the English seaside town rightwing influencers say is being ‘invaded’ Some in Dover say their town is being exploited by content creators and politicians, but others claim there is a genuine problem Kevin Rawlinson Sat 1 Aug 2026 07.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 07.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google I f you believe rightwing influencers and politicians, Dover and the wider Kent coast has been the site of an “invasion” for years now. And, for an online audience of millions, they and their camera crews have been the vanguard in the nation’s defence. Indeed, if you believe all you see on the algorithms of amateur Channel watchers, the shadow home secretary, Chris Philp , braved a hail of French gunfire as he took to the water in a fishing boat this week; an attempt by the French authorities, he suggested, to deter him in his mission of highlighting the small boats crisis. The inconvenient truth behind Philp’s attempt to self-police our borders is that nothing of the sort happened. The French government said he simply passed by a routine training exercise that involved firing live rounds. With its sloping pebble beach and sunbathers and dog-walkers enjoying the summer sunshine by its marina this week, Dover does not look much like the frontline of a war zone. Are the rightwing figures who regularly visit the town to create social media content exploiting it for their own careers, or are they seeking solutions to a genuine problem? “They’re using Dover a bit,” said one resident, Alison Drake. “People making all these videos and that is not really doing much, is it?” View image in fullscreen The frontline of a war zone? The Dover seafront, where rightwing influencers and politicians flock to make content for social media about an ‘invasion’. Photograph: Andrew Aitchison/The Guardian Some said that creating tension where there was none before was all part of the plan. “What they’re trying to do is play on fear with all of these stunts,” said Razia Shariff, who runs the Kent Refugee Action Network (Kran), a charity that provides education for refugee and asylum-seeking young people. Whether or not the selfie stick-toting influencers who descend on the south coast need to capture the supposed “invasion” is, for some, a moot point. Some of those living in the area insisted the relentless focus on the issue – and on the region – was at least keeping the problem in the public eye. “They’re letting the people know that the French are not doing anything,” Tom Armstrong said. Armstrong is avowedly anti-immigration and said the “country is being devalued” by it. He said rightwing politicians were helping that cause. “You’ve got to draw attention,” he said. Later, he added: “We’ve got to know the truth.” Philp claimed to have been exposing the small boats crisis during his jaunt across the Channel. While Drake agreed that rightwing figures highlighting the issue might prompt action, she added: “Everyone knows about it, it’s about time they did something about it. They don’t do anything. So, it’s all very well everyone keep going on about it, but no one does anything. They know it’s happening.” View image in fullscreen Alison Drake said despite the attention on Dover, no one was doing anything about the small boat crossings. Photograph: Andrew Aitchison/The Guardian Few people have had more opportunity to solve the small boats crisis than Philp who, as immigration minister in the early 2020s, oversaw a sharp increase in crossings. In contrast, organisations such as Kran are working to alleviate some of the challenges caused by the way migration has been handled by successive governments. The young people Kran helps are taking part in a summer scheme at an academy in Kent this week. Shariff spoke glowingly of some of their predecessors’ achievements. One, she said, had arrived in the UK as a child refugee and now worked as a nurse in local hospitals. “Others have set up their own businesses against all the odds. They get on with their lives and they try.” Carol, who lives in Dover and did not want to give her surname, suggested the focus should be more on the work of organisations such as Kran than on politicians such as Philp and Nigel Farage . The Reform leader has repeatedly referred to small boat crossings as an “invasion”. Standing on the Dover seafront in 2024, he described the site as the “frontline of the great national debate on immigration”. Carol did not recognise the picture the Reform leader painted of the town, as she stood on almost the same spot he had occupied two years ago. “I mean, look, it’s pleasant enough,” she said, nodding towards the beach. View image in fullscreen Carol worries that Dover being used as the backdrop for content about small boat crossings could deter tourists from visiting. Photograph: Andrew Aitchison/The Guardian People there were sunbathing in the warm weather, while children played in the water and others took an opportunity to go out in the sea in small vessels. “I think it is unfair that Dover is headlined in that way. Because you can sit on the beach, enjoy the area.” Carol said it was frustrating that Dover and other nearby towns were so often used as the backdrop for social media content focusing on the small boats crisis and feared it could deter people from visiting an area that needs a lift. “It’s a bit rundown, like many towns. It’s a bit sad. So it’s not a great place to shop, by all means, but the seafront’s lovely. And the surrounding countryside is lovely. I’m sure it isn’t helping. Dover has got that image.” Explore more on these topics Immigration and asylum Kent Chris Philp Nigel Farage news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story French riot police used teargas on people trying to board small boat, charity claims ICE-linked security firm reports UK revenue slump after asylum contract ends Home Office used ‘AI hallucinated’ information to refuse asylum claim, judge suggests Tory MP accuses French navy of firing ‘warning’ shots near him in Channel Home Office blocking evacuation of dozens of women and children from Gaza UK to continue sending potential trafficking victims to France despite court ruling Immigration bill amendment will allow removal of Rochdale gang leader Mahmood’s cutting of protections for UK-France ‘one in, one out’ asylum deal ruled unlawful Jamaican man who has lived in UK for 26 years facing deportation No 10 shares ‘public’s shock’ at reports of convicted people smuggler living in UK Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

https://www.dw.com/en/russian-strike-on-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Jc0O Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country 'cannot be left alone in finding solutions to defend against' such drone strikes Image: Ukrainian Emergency Service/AFP Advertisement At least 37 people were killed after a Russian drone strike on a ammunition depot near Kyiv late Friday, one of the deadliest attacks in Ukraine this year. The drone strike was the second attack to hit an arms depot near the Ukrainian capital in less than two months. "A terrible situation and terrible negligence on the part of those who stored explosives right next to people," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a video address on X. "Another such crime — after what happened in Vyshneve — is absolutely unacceptable," he added. Zelenskyy was referring to an attack on an ammunition warehouse last month that set off secondary explosions in the small town on Kyiv's western outskirts, killing ten people. Russia and Ukraine have recently intensified long-range strikes, increasingly hitting civilian infrastructure such as logistics warehouses and oil and port facilities. These attacks have resulted in more civilian casualties. What else do we know about the Russian drone attack near Kyiv? The strike sparked a major fire and explosions at the arms depot in the Bucha district, close to the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv, forcing more than 370 people to evacuate the region. Dozens were injured. Among those killed was Taras Didych, head of the Dmytrivka community, who was one of the first to rush to the scene to rescue people, according to Kyiv region governor Tymur Tkachenko. He also said the attack damaged at least 50 residential buildings. Zelenskyy earlier said that criminal proceedings had been opened on charges of official negligence. "There are regulations in place — ammunition cannot be stored near homes or other residential areas," Zelenskyy said. Kyiv under jet-powered drone attacks Friday's drone attack followed ​two days of constant air raids aimed at the Ukrainian capital and the surrounding region. "Kyiv is under virtually nonstop attack from jet-powered drones. Ukraine cannot be left alone in finding solutions to defend against such strikes," said Zelenskyy, adding that Russia also struck nine other regions overnight. It's been more than four and a half years since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of its neighbor . Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko and Wesley Dockery Don't let the algorithm hide the news. https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/bus-carry.text: Jakub Krupa and agencies Updated Sun, August 16, 2026 at 11:15 AM UTC 0 Emergency services at the scene of the crash near the town of Mezőkeresztes.Photograph: Balazs Toth/Mezőkövesd Képekben/Reuters Twelve people have died after a bus carrying a group of Polish tourists overturned on the M3 motorway in Hungary on the way back from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Local police said the bus crashed near the town of Mezőkeresztes after it “went off the straight road into a ditch and overturned” at 1am local time. Early reports suggested the driver had probably fallen asleep. He survived the crash and was taken into custody. The bus was carrying a group of pilgrims from Poland’s south-eastern Podkarpackie region who were returning from a pilgrimage to the Catholic shrine in Međugorje, in southern Bosnia and Herzegovina, with 57 passengers and two drivers onboard. Poland’s foreign ministry said “virtually all” passengers were transferred to local hospitals in Eger, Debrecen and Miskolc, and 10 people were in a serious condition. The Hungarian ambulance service said 37 people sustained minor injuries. Polish and Hungarian leaders expressed their condolences after the crash. Poland’s president, Karol Nawrocki, said: “With deep sorrow, I received the tragic news of the accident involving a Polish bus in Hungary, in which so many of our compatriots perished. “In the face of this unimaginable tragedy, which has touched us all, I join in prayer and profound compassion with the families and loved ones of the victims.” Hungary’s prime minister, Péter Magyar, expressed his “sincere condolences to the families of the victims” and thanked the emergency services involved in the rescue operation. Poland’s infrastructure minister, Dariusz Klimczak, said the general inspectorate of road transport would conduct enhanced checks on all buses and drivers’ working hours. The owner of the bus company involved in the crash told Business Insider Polska that the vehicle “was driven by two experienced drivers”. The investigation into the crash will be led by a group of Polish prosecutors from the south-eastern town of Krosno, the prosecutors’ office said in a statement. Međugorje, despite some doubts about its religious history , is a popular summer destination for Polish Catholics. In 2022, 12 people died and 30 were injured when a bus carrying Polish pilgrims to Međugorje crashed in Croatia . In 2002, 20 Polish pilgrims died and 31 were injured in a bus crash in Hungary. https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/21/puti.text: Vladimir Putin's United Russia party has won a record supermajority in parliament, preliminary results showed Monday. The tightly controlled three-day vote excluded every party critical of the Kremlin or the war in Ukraine.Central Election Commission chief Ella Pamfilova said United Russia had secured 355 of the State Duma's 450 seats. That beats its previous record of 343, set in 2016, and is well above the 301 needed to change the constitution. Final results are due later this week.The Communist Party came second with 40 seats, followed by the nationalist LDPR on 25, New People on 20 and A Just Russia on four. Pamfilova put turnout at more than 59 percent.It was Russia's first parliamentary election since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Criticism of the war is banned, and Yabloko, the only party calling for an end to the fighting, was barred from running for the national parliament, though it was allowed to stand in some regional votes."These indicators, of course, point to the highest level of consolidation within Russian society around the head of state," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.United Russia told state media that 49 veterans who fought in Ukraine are expected to enter the Duma for the party.Voting also took place in occupied parts of Ukraine, including Crimea and the Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia regions.On Sunday, the final day of voting, Kyiv hit Moscow with its biggest drone attack of the war, killing two people and setting an oil refinery ablaze. Russia's defence ministry accused Ukraine of trying to disrupt the vote and vowed to intensify strikes on Kyiv.Russia's 'veneer of democracy'The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said the Kremlin had "silenced dissent" and shut out international election monitors."The veneer of democracy is all that remains in Russia," she said. "The State Duma elections held by Russia on 18–20 September underscored the continued and deepening erosion of democracy in Russia, taking place in an increasingly authoritarian political environment."In a statement on behalf of the bloc, Kallas said the EU would impose sanctions on those who organised the vote or stood as candidates in occupied Ukrainian territory."The European Union reiterates that it does not and will never recognise either the holding of these so-called “elections” in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine or their results." the statement said.Britain, Australia, Canada, New Zealand and Norway said in a joint statement that holding the election in occupied areas was a "gross violation" of Ukraine's sovereignty and the UN Charter. They said the vote could not change the status of those territories under international law."These sham elections are part of a wider system of occupation: the imposition of Russian administration, law, media, education, language and citizenship, backed by coercion and repression," the statement said.Ukraine's foreign ministry had earlier called the voting in occupied regions a "farce" and said it would not recognise the results.The election brought one surprise. In the Novgorod region, where it was allowed on the ballot for regional elections held at the same time, Yabloko won just over six percent of the vote, enough to enter the regional parliament.Putin's political opponents are in exile, in prison or dead. His main rival, Alexei Navalny, died in an Arctic prison in 2024.
